newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy PM likely to avoid early clash on pensions.
newsitem.headline: Italy PM likely to avoid early clash on pensions.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi is likely to bend over backwards to avoid an early clash with hard left allies and union leaders over proposed cuts to Italy's hefty pensions bill, analysts said on Wednesday.

Prodi has been putting the finishing touches to a three-year economic plan, due to be released on Friday, setting out tax and spending plans for the next three years in a gamble to put Italy in the starting line-up for Europe's planned single currency.

Trades unions and the government's hard left allies do not like what they know of the plans, but analysts said the government will try and avoid a showdown over the sensitive area of pension provision for the time being.
"These people are in government because they want to stay where they are. They don't want to commit suicide," said Giovanna Mossetti, an economist at Milan brokerage Caboto.

Prodi may have no choice but to keep vague all references in the plan to reform Italy's ungainly system of pensions and welfare, known as the DPEF, if he wants to avert a full-blown crisis, analysts say.
"The DPEF has to be a bit vague but it will be a first attempt at reaching a compromise on pensions," said Riccardo Barbieri, an economist with Morgan Stanley in London.
The real battle over pensions reform is likely to be postponed until the autumn when the government sends its 1998 budget plans to parliament.
The loudest protests have come from Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the Communist Refoundation party on whose votes the government relies for a majority in parliament's lower house.
Bertinotti has said the three-year plan should make no mention of cutting the state pensions bill, which the government says is growing at an unsustainable rate.
The government's rolling economic strategy, updated every year, traditionally sets budgetary targets for three years ahead but avoids details on how savings will be achieved.

This year is different. The government has set its sights on lowering the public sector deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 -- a target it must meet to have any chance of joining European Economic and Monetary Union.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi is determined to send a signal in this year's DPEF that Italy can lower the deficit even further next year and he also wants to make public how the government intends to meet that target.

The DPEF will form the basis of a so-called convergence plan, laying down how Italy plans to keep public finances on a tight leash in coming years, which the government has promised to send to the European Union's executive Commission next month.
Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the CISL trade union confederation, said on Wednesday the government was putting too much emphasis on spending cuts in its 1998 budget plans.
The government wanted to cut the public sector deficit by 25 trillion lire next year ($14.9 billion), with two-thirds coming from spending cuts and one third from increased revenue, D'Antoni said.
A union official also said the government is aiming to cut the deficit-to-GDP ratio to 2.8 percent next year.
D'Antoni and other top union leaders were informally briefed about the DPEF by Prodi on Tuesday evening.
Although the government did not discuss cuts in social welfare spending at Tuesday's meeting, D'Antoni said hefty spending cuts were bound to affect welfare provision.
"It is clear the more you cut spending the more you have to cut social (welfare) spending," he said.
Newspapers have reported the government has earmarked eight trillion lire of cuts in spending on pensions, health care and welfare next year -- a figure the unions say is unacceptable.
The government may have to scale down its ambitions by quoting a lower number in the DPEF, possibly five trillion lire.
It has the option of revising its plans later in the year when it drafts the 1998 budget because the only figure in the DPEF which is legally binding is the overall budget target.
